claims.claim: An outlier is an observation that lies an abnormal distance from other values in a sample; deciding what counts as abnormal is a judgment left to the analyst.
An outlier may be bad data (recorded or entered incorrectly) or a genuine observation (random variation or something scientifically interesting).
Outliers should be investigated carefully before any decision; they often contain valuable information about the process under study or about the data-gathering and recording process.
Summaries computed from every value, such as the average, are sensitive to extreme observations; methods designed not to be unduly affected by outliers are called robust.
When an outlying value is confirmed erroneous it should be corrected or removed from the analysis; when it cannot be confirmed erroneous, analysts typically should not simply delete it.
Before considering elimination of an outlier, analysts should try to understand why it appeared and whether similar values are likely to continue to appear.
Different statistical software uses different rules for flagging outliers, and some datasets naturally contain extreme values that are not problems.
Outlier handling is a documented decision: verify the value, correct it if wrong, keep it with a note, or analyze with and without it — and never delete silently.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Should flagged outliers be deleted automatically?
positions: Some automated cleaning pipelines drop flagged outliers as part of routine data preparation.
NIST guidance holds that analysts typically do not want to simply delete an outlying observation and should investigate before considering elimination.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NIST: outliers are investigated first, and deletion is legitimate only with evidence and documentation. Automatic deletion is presented as a risky shortcut, not a default.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which rule decides whether a value counts as an outlier?
positions: Different software and textbooks use different formulas (for example, distance from quartiles) to flag outliers.
The definition itself leaves what counts as 'abnormal' to the analyst's judgment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: At literacy level the lesson avoids formulas entirely and presents outlier status as a judgment call supported by rules of thumb; box-plot and fence rules belong to the visualization sibling topic.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.3.5.17. Detection of Outliers (Exploratory Data Analysis)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live section page directly on 2026-08-21. Supports: an outlier as an observation that appears to deviate markedly from other observations; outliers may indicate bad data (coded incorrectly, experiment not run correctly) and confirmed erroneous values should be deleted or corrected; outliers may also be random variation or scientifically interesting; analysts typically do not want to simply delete the outlying observation; significant outliers may call for robust statistical techniques; and the labeling/accommodation/identification framework for outliers (Iglewicz and Hoaglin). Facts synthesized into original prose; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Read directly (web edition) on 2026-08-21.
